extraction.name: SciQ
extraction.description: SciQ is a dataset of 13.7K multiple choice science exam questions assembled using a novel crowdsourcing method. The method leverages a large corpus of domain-specific text and a small set of existing questions, producing model suggestions for document selection and answer distractor choice to aid human question generation. The dataset includes a multiple choice version and a direct answer version, and has been shown to improve accuracy on real science exams when used as additional training data.
extraction.creator: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, Matt Gardner
extraction.citeAs: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, and Matt Gardner. 2017. Crowdsourcing Multiple Choice Science Questions. arXiv preprint arXiv:1707.06209.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The data collection process involved a two-step crowdsourcing method. First, crowd workers were presented with a set of candidate passages (filtered from science study textbooks) and asked to choose one to formulate a question that could be answered by the passage. Second, another worker took the generated question and correct answer, and produced three distractors, aided by a model trained to predict good answer distractors. This shifted the human intelligence task from purely generative to a selection, modification, and validation task.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The base corpus for question generation consisted of science study textbooks from CK-12 and OpenStax, covering biology, chemistry, earth science, and physics, spanning elementary to college introductory material. The distractor model was trained on a set of 3705 science exam questions (4th and 8th grade).
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A rule-based document filter model was used to preprocess the base corpus. Individual paragraphs were fed into the system, which classified individual sentences and accepted a paragraph if a minimum number of sentences were accepted. Filter rules included lexical, grammatical, pragmatical, and complexity-based criteria to identify simple declarative statements and filter out irrelevant content.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The collected data underwent several preprocessing steps. A rule-based document filter was applied to the base corpus to select relevant paragraphs for question generation. For the distractor selection task, a model trained on real science exam questions was used to predict good answer distractors, which were then presented as suggestions to crowd workers.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol:
The annotation process involved two main tasks performed by crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk. 
1. Question Formulation Task: Workers were presented with three filtered textbook paragraphs and chose one (or rejected all) to formulate a question. Instructions specified desirable characteristics: no yes/no questions, not requiring further context, querying general principles, question length 6-30 words, answer length up to 3 words, no ambiguous questions, and answers clear from the paragraph. Examples of desirable and undesirable questions were provided.
2. Distractor Selection Task: Workers received a question-answer pair from the first task and the top six distractors suggested by a model. They first judged if the question was suitable for a school science exam. Then, they selected up to two suggested distractors and were required to write at least one distractor themselves, ensuring a total of three distractors. Examples of desirable and undesirable distractors were given.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: In the question formulation task, 12.1% of the cases resulted in all three presented documents being rejected by workers. In the distractor selection task, 92.8% of the questions passed the quality control check (judged suitable for a school science exam). Crowd workers accepted model-predicted distractors around half of the time, with 36.1% of the distractors in the final dataset being model-generated. A qualitative evaluation showed that humans identified crowdsourced questions from original science exam questions in 55% of cases, which was not statistically significant from random guessing.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each item consists of one question, one correct answer, and three distractors (incorrect answer options).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: A total of 175 workers participated in the crowdsourcing project. Workers were required to have Master’s status on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A noisy classifier was used to find relevant passages for the first task. For the second task, a distractor model, implemented using scikit-learn’s random forest with default parameters (500 trees, at least 4 samples per tree leaf), was trained to predict plausible answer distractors. This model used features such as GloVe embeddings, POS-tag consistency, singular/plural consistency, word frequency, Levenshtein distance, suffix consistency, token overlap, length similarity, numerical content indicators, unit of measure indicators, WordNet-based hypernymy indicators, and KB-based connections via OpenIE triples.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to address the lack of large in-domain training sets for science exam Question Answering (QA), a high-level NLP task requiring information extraction, reading comprehension, and common sense reasoning. By providing a larger dataset, it facilitates progress in applying sophisticated statistical techniques, particularly neural models, to science QA, which has implications for educational applications and AI development in targeted domains.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is useful for studying reading comprehension models in medium-data settings (tens of thousands of examples, not hundreds of thousands), as neural models did not outperform simple information retrieval baselines on the multiple choice version. A small percentage of the passages used for the direct answer version were obtained from unreleasable texts, resulting in a slightly smaller direct answer dataset.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, testing, and validation of machine learning models, particularly for science exam Question Answering. It can be used as additional training data to improve model performance on real science exams. It supports two main usage scenarios: a multiple choice version (selecting the correct answer given a question and options) and a direct answer version (predicting the answer span within a given passage for a question).
